message.content:
I don’t have a way to probe your connection from here, so I can’t tell you the exact download/upload speeds you’re getting right now.  
But you can check it yourself in a few quick ways:

---

## 1️⃣ Web‑based Speed Test (easiest)

1. Open a web browser.  
2. Go to <https://www.speedtest.net> (or <https://fast.com> for a very quick test).  
3. Click “Go” (or “Start” on Fast.com).  
4. The page will automatically ping a nearby server and show you:
   * **Download speed** (Mbps)
   * **Upload speed** (Mbps)
   * **Latency** (ms)

---

## 2️⃣ Command‑Line Speed Test (Windows)

If you prefer the command line, you can use the free `speedtest-cli` tool.  
Below are the steps to install it (via `pip`) and run a test.

### 2.1 Install `speedtest-cli`

```powershell
# Open PowerShell as Administrator
pip install speedtest-cli
```

If you don’t have `pip` installed, you can install it by downloading the [Python installer](https://www.python.org/downloads/) and selecting “Add Python to PATH” during installation.

### 2.2 Run a Simple Test

```powershell
speedtest-cli --simple
```

This will output something like:

```
Ping: 12.34 ms
Download: 123.45 Mbit/s
Upload: 67.89 Mbit/s
```

---

## 3️⃣ Quick PowerShell One‑Liner (No Installation)

If you don’t want to install anything, you can run a quick PowerShell one‑liner that downloads a file from a public CDN and measures the time. It’s not as accurate as a dedicated speed test, but it gives a rough idea.

```powershell
$uri = "https://speed.hetzner.de/100MB.bin"
$start = Get-Date
(New-Object System.Net.WebClient).DownloadFile($uri, "$env:TEMP\tempfile.bin")
$end = Get-Date
$elapsed = ($end - $start).TotalSeconds
$sizeMB = 100
$downloadSpeed = [math]::Round(($sizeMB / $elapsed), 2)
Write-Host "Approx. download speed: $downloadSpeed MB/s"
```

> **Note:** This script downloads a 100 MB file from Hetzner’s CDN. Delete the downloaded file afterward (`Remove-Item "$env:TEMP\tempfile.bin"`).

---

## 4️⃣ Mobile Apps

If you’re on a phone, most carriers provide a built‑in speed‑test app, or you can download the official Speedtest app from Google Play / App Store.

---

### Quick Summary

| Method | How to Use | Pros | Cons |
|--------|------------|------|------|
| Speedtest.net | Browser | Very accurate, easy | Requires internet |
| speedtest-cli | PowerShell | Accurate, scriptable | Needs Python/pip |
| PowerShell one‑liner | PowerShell | No install | Rough estimate |
| Mobile app | Phone | Convenient | Depends on device |

Pick the one that fits your workflow. Once you run the test, you’ll see your current download/upload speeds and latency. If you notice speeds far below what your ISP promises, you might want to contact them or troubleshoot your network.
